ut_willy_wall.blurb: Willy Wall is a small, fairly recent sport wall in Maple Canyon, central Utah, facing Rock Island from the opposite side of the canyon road. Ten bolted lines span easy 5.7s up through the low 5.11s, and the bulk of them sit in the 5.11 range, so it suits climbers who are comfortable pulling hard on the grade rather than those still building up. The wall sits in shade for most of the day, which helps when the canyon heats up. Its base is a sloping hillside with little flat ground, so keep your pack tidy. Because it is compact, it works well as a short add-on to a day elsewhere in the canyon.

ut_watchman_the.blurb: The Watchman is the big sandstone peak at the south end of Zion National Park, and its west face holds a handful of long traditional lines. The face is about half a mile across and well over a thousand feet tall, cut by cracks, corners, pillars and chimneys, with the steeper, more solid rock toward the south end. Climbs here are tall multi-pitch crack routes in the 5.10 to 5.12 range, so prior multi-pitch sandstone experience matters. Expect loose rock on ledges and in the wide chimneys. The place sees few visitors, and the sandstone is fragile when damp, so wait for it to dry fully after rain.

ut_the_left_hand_fork_ice_climbs.blurb: This is one of the winter ice zones of Maple Canyon in central Utah, found where the canyon splits into three and you take the south-heading branch. Around ten lines form here, most of them water ice from moderate WI3 up to WI5, plus two mixed routes: an easy, well-protected introduction to mixed climbing and one much harder test piece. The flows build from snowmelt that refreezes, so a snowy, cold winter is needed. The road is usually snow-covered through the season, so plan on walking or skinning in for a fair distance before the first flow.

ut_the_right_hand_fork_ice_climbs.blurb: The Right Hand Fork is an ice area in Maple Canyon, central Utah, reached by following the main road to the point where three canyons meet and bearing right. About ten lines form here, spanning easy WI2 steps to serious WI5 and WI5-6 pillars, with the middle and upper grades well represented. A few lines have a trad, alpine or mixed flavour. Ice depends on snowmelt freezing again, so it needs a snowy, cold winter, and the road is normally snow-covered, which makes hiking or skinning in the standard approach. Several of the harder lines have a serious reputation, so treat conditions with respect.

ut_toadstool.blurb: Toadstool is a boulder in Mario Land, a quieter satellite zone of Moe's Valley outside St. George, Utah. Around ten problems are known here, running from an easy V2 through a cluster of V4 and V5 lines to a couple of hard testpieces at V8 and V9, so mid-grade climbers get the most out of it. The best-known line is a traverse around the boulder, which fits the traverse-heavy character of this part of the valley. Mario Land is described as similar to the rest of Moe's but with fewer people, making it a good alternative on busy weekends. Winter is the usual season for bouldering here.

ut_right_side_cragging.blurb: Right Side Cragging is the biggest sub-area on the sunny side of Day Canyon, a side canyon off Potash Road near Moab, Utah. The canyon feels quite different from the surrounding desert: walls begin small and grow large as you walk in, and it is quiet and scenic compared with the busier Wall Street. Climbing is mostly traditional, with a few sport lines and a boulder problem, and most routes fall between about 5.9 and 5.11, with an easy 5.4 as well. The sandstone is delicate when wet, so give it plenty of time to dry after rain before pulling on it.

ut_plumb_line_gully.blurb: Plumb Line Gully is a compact collection of about ten routes in Little Cottonwood Canyon, tucked just east of The Thumb near Gate Buttress, roughly a mile up the canyon. It is almost all traditional climbing, with one bolted sport line, and grades run from 5.7 through the 5.10s into the low 5.11s, with the 5.10 and 5.11 lines making up most of it. The wall is a little short of vertical, and the gully offers a good variety of lines for a small area. Several climbs face different ways, so a route that is in the sun will often have a neighbour in shade.
